title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Small bowel bleeding compromises 5% to 10% of all GI bleeds. The etiology is extensive and poses a diagnostic challenge for physicians. To avoid the high morbidity and mortality associated with this condition, it must be promptly diagnosed and treated. This activity reviews the evaluation and treatment of small bowel bleeding and highlights the interprofessional team's role in evaluating and treating patients with this condition.

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Introduction
content: Gastrointestinal bleeding is the most common diagnosis among inpatient admissions related to the gastrointestinal tract. Amongst the gastrointestinal bleeds, about 50% are due to upper gastrointestinal tract bleeds, 40% are due to lower gastrointestinal tract bleeds, and about 5% to 10% are due to lesions in the small bowel. [1] The small bowel is the part of the gastrointestinal tract between the ligament of Treitz and the ileocecal valve. Small bowel bleeding can be divided into overt or occult. [2]

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Introduction
content: Patients are considered to have overt bleeding when they have visible bleeding, either melena or hematochezia. The bleeding is considered occult when there is no gross bleeding, but signs and symptoms of anemia, including fatigue, dyspnea, or palpitations, are present. Small bowel bleeding poses a significant diagnostic challenge for gastroenterologists. The clinical significance lies in the fact that most small bowel causes go undetected because the small bowel is long and difficult to reach, making it difficult to evaluate. [3] [4]

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Etiology
content: The etiology of small bowel bleeding is broad and varies with patient age. [5] Patients under the age of 40 are likely to have a Dieulafoy lesion, a neoplasm, a Meckel diverticulum, or an inflammatory bowel disease. In patients older than 40 years, angiodysplasia, Dieulafoy lesions, or NSAID-related ulcers are more likely. [6]

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Etiology
content: The most common cause of small bowel gastrointestinal bleed is a vascular lesion. 30-40% of bleeding in the small bowel is caused by abnormal vessels in the small bowel, with angiodysplasia being the most common. [7] The vascular lesions may also be induced by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The other causes include tumors, aorto-enteric fistula, medications, small intestine ulcers, and non-specific enteritis. [8]

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Epidemiology
content: The prevalence of small bowel lesions has been estimated to be 5 to 10% in patients presenting with gastrointestinal bleeding. [9] The studies have shown neoplasms to be the most common cause in Asian countries. In contrast, angiectasias were the leading cause in Western countries. [10] The type of lesion causing the bleed depends on the patient's age. Crohn disease and Meckel diverticulum are more likely in the younger population, less than 40 years. Angiectasia and vascular lesions are most commonly observed in individuals older than 40 years. Neoplasms and Dieulafoy lesions are observed with equal frequency in both younger and older age groups. [11] There is no role of gender, and prevalence is equal in males and females. There is limited data on small bowel findings across ethnicities.

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- History and Physical
content: The patient's initial assessment with small bowel bleeding must include a good clinical history and physical examination. A small bowel bleed can present with a range of manifestations. It can be overt or occult bleeding. It can be a massive bleed, presenting as shock, or it could be persistent bleeding leading to anemia. A detailed history can help guide toward a specific diagnosis. [12] [13] It should include the following, Medical history (valvular heart disease, liver cirrhosis, chronic pancreatitis, radiation therapy) Surgical history (liver transplantation, abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, bowel resection) Medications (NSAIDs, anticoagulants, antiplatelets) Family history (Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, Peutz-Jegher syndrome) Social history (alcohol intake)

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- History and Physical
content: The physical examination findings can help to narrow down the diagnosis. The findings of telangiectasia in HHT (hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia), spider angioma, and caput medusa in portal hypertension, and pigmented lips in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome can be found on examination. [14]

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- History and Physical
content: The history of chronic pancreatitis can lead to the diagnosis of rare causes like Haemosuccus pancreaticus . [15] Additional causes, such as a history of worms in the stool, should be sought in individuals, particularly in tropical regions.

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Evaluation
content: Small intestinal bleeding is a rare cause of gastrointestinal bleeding. The diagnosis is challenging for the physician and requires substantial time and imposes a financial burden. The initial step in evaluation is endoscopy. However, with the advancement in novel endoscopic and radiological techniques, diagnosis and treatment have evolved. The latest diagnostic modalities, including capsule endoscopy and deep enteroscopy, have enabled deeper visualization of the small bowel, facilitating the diagnosis and treatment of lesions. [13] There is no single diagnostic test with high sensitivity and specificity, making the diagnosis challenging.

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Evaluation -- Endoscopy
content: Endoscopy is the first diagnostic study. A regular endoscope helps evaluate the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum. It is capable of providing a good view up to the first part of the small bowel. It has the advantage of being both diagnostic and therapeutic. The endoscopist can perform an intervention if a lesion is found. [16]

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: Computed tomography enterography typically uses an oral contrast agent. It allows detailed inspection of the small bowel lining and the search for lesions. [17] The advantage of computed tomography scanning is the ability to identify the bleeding source beyond the standard endoscope's reach. The primary limitation is the inability to perform any intervention, even when an abnormality is identified. Another imaging modality, computed tomography angiography, helps in localizing the lesion and embolizing it. A disadvantage of computed tomography angiography is that the lesion must be actively bleeding, with a bleeding rate of 0.3 to 0.5 mL/min. [18] Nuclear studies, including scintigraphy with tagged RBC scans, are more sensitive than computed tomography angiography. It can detect bleeding at a rate of 0.1 mL/min. [19]

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Evaluation -- Capsule Endoscopy
content: Capsule endoscopy is used when endoscopy studies have failed to identify a bleeding source. The camera is attached to a device approximately the size of a pill. It helps visualize the entire gastrointestinal tract by acquiring images until the material is finally eliminated in the stool. [20]

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Evaluation -- Capsule Endoscopy
content: The capsule study is generally safe. It has the advantage of visualizing the entire gastrointestinal tract and localizing the bleeding source. The disadvantages include the inability to take biopsies and do any intervention. In patients with a history of abdominal surgery, the capsule can rarely become lodged in the gastrointestinal tract. It may require surgery if the capsule gets stuck. Despite these limitations, capsule endoscopy is the second-line test if the standard endoscope fails to identify a bleeding source. [21]

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Evaluation -- Push Enteroscopy
content: Push enteroscopy and double-balloon enteroscopy are recent advances over standard endoscopes. They have been used when the lesion is located farther down in the small bowel and is not visible with standard endoscopes. It uses 2 balloons, which can help advance the scope further into the small bowel. [22] It is possible to see the lesions, as far as the ileum, depending upon the performer's expertise. The advantage is the ability to perform treatment, obtain biopsies, and mark the area with a tattoo. Studies have shown that the enteroscope has identified the bleeding source in approximately 74% of patients and treated approximately 60%-70%. [23]

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Evaluation -- Intraoperative Enteroscopy
content: Surgery may be required when no diagnosis can be made. Intraoperative enteroscopy is done under general anesthesia by a team comprising gastroenterologists and surgeons. The scope is advanced through the incision in the small bowel. The advantage is that it allows treatment of the cause of bleeding, AVMs, or the removal of masses or polyps. It has been shown to treat about 70% of the patients effectively. [24]

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Treatment / Management
content: The management options for small bowel bleeding involve conservative, radiological, pharmacological, endoscopic, and surgical methods. The choice depends upon the indications, availability, and expertise. [25] The occult bleeding is usually treated in the outpatient setting. It involves endoscopic and imaging studies to localize the lesion and treat it appropriately. The overt bleeding is usually an emergency and warrants inpatient admission. It requires fluid resuscitation and localization of the lesion using angiography and scintigraphy. Enteroscopy could be used for therapeutic management once the lesion has been identified.

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Treatment / Management
content: Pharmacological therapies are used when lesions are extensive and cannot be treated with invasive therapies. The different pharmacological options include hormonal therapies (estrogen and progesterone) and octreotide. [26] Octreotide is effective in various studies. These drugs act through multiple mechanisms, including decreased splanchnic blood flow, enhanced platelet aggregation, and inhibition of angiogenesis. [27] Thalidomide, a VEGF inhibitor, acts by inhibiting angiogenesis. It has been used for refractory and recurrent blood loss secondary to angiodysplasia. [28] Studies have shown that patients who took this drug had a reduced need for blood transfusions.

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Treatment / Management
content: Endoscopic and interventional radiographic techniques are used to treat vascular lesions. The choice of the appropriate therapy depends on the availability and expertise. The options include electrocoagulation, laser photocoagulation, argon plasma coagulation (APC), injection sclerotherapy, hemoclip placement, endoscopic band ligation, and/or a combination of these. [29] [30] Endoscopic hemostatic methods are used for ectopic varices. Interventional radiology techniques, including embolization, are performed when endoscopic treatment is unsuccessful. [31] Surgery is the last resort and is done in patients with recurrent bleeding and failed endoscopic treatments.

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis for small bowel bleeding includes: Inflammatory bowel disease Meckel's diverticulum Gastrointestinal stromal cell tumor Polypoid lesions Dieulafoy lesions Angioectasia NSAID ulcers Haemobilia Haemosuccus pancreaticus Aorto-enteric fistula

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Prognosis
content: There are limited studies regarding the prognosis after a small bowel bleed. The in-hospital mortality is low (< 5%). Most complications occur in patients with comorbidities. [32] Death usually occurs due to the worsening of underlying co-morbidities. Increasing age has been shown to be associated with increased mortality. [33] The mortality rate was higher in men than in women. The negative prognostic factors involve hypovolemia, transfusion requirement, and underlying coagulopathies. Long-term follow-up studies are limited for small bowel bleeding. [34]

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Complications
content: Complications of small bowel bleeding include: Heart failure Respiratory distress Myocardial infarction Infection Shock Death

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients should be educated about the manifestations of gastrointestinal bleeding. They should be made aware of presentations such as melena and signs of anemia, including fatigue, palpitations, and dyspnea. Counseling should be provided to limit the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and to quit smoking and alcohol. [35] If concerned about changes in bowel habits or any overt or occult gastrointestinal bleeding, they should follow up with their local physician. Patients should be educated about concerning scenarios, such as hypotension or confusion. They should be made aware of the need for emergent management in these conditions.

title: Small Bowel Bleeding -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Patients typically present to their primary care physician with anemia-like symptoms and to the emergency department with hematochezia. Management typically employs an interprofessional approach that includes surgeons, gastroenterologists, radiologists, and intensivists, supported by nursing staff trained in gastrointestinal disorders. [36] Depending on the presentation, they may require ICU monitoring. Some patients may require fluid resuscitation and blood transfusions. Multiple imaging studies might be required before the diagnosis is made. [37] Coordinating these activities through an interprofessional team approach improves patient outcomes.

[38] The outcomes depend upon the patient's age, underlying co-morbidities, hemodynamic stability, and the need for emergent surgery.
